name: Sumatran Tiger
description: The Sumatran tiger is the smallest surviving tiger subspecies in the world, found exclusively on the island of Sumatra. They are easily distinguished by their darker orange coat and narrower, more closely spaced stripes compared to other tiger species. These majestic cats are highly adapted to the dense tropical rainforests and swampy areas of their native habitat. They are solitary hunters that rely on stealth and camouflage to ambush their prey in the thick undergrowth. Unfortunately, they are critically endangered due to habitat loss and poaching for their skin and body parts.
facts: They are excellent swimmers and often use water to cool down or hunt.
Their stripes are unique to each individual, like a human fingerprint.
They are the only surviving tiger species in Indonesia after the extinction of the Balinese and Javan tigers.
population_estimate: ~600 mature individuals (critically endangered with stable breeding in Leuser ecosystem)

name: Sumatran Rhino
description: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the smallest and hairiest of all living rhino species, evolved for life in deep tropical forests. They possess a distinctive appearance with a layer of reddish-brown hair covering their skin. These rhinos are browsers that feed on a wide variety of forest plant life, including shoots and young leaves. They are known to be very solitary animals that communicate using scent markers and vocalizations. Currently, they are among the most endangered mammals on Earth, with very few individuals remaining in the wild.
facts: They are the only Asian rhino species with two horns.
They spend a large portion of their day wallowing in mud holes to keep cool and protect their skin.
They are highly solitary animals and communicate primarily through scent and sound.
population_estimate: ~34-47 individuals (critically endangered - IUCN 2024 estimate)

name: Javan Rhino
description: The Javan rhinoceros is one of the rarest large mammals on the planet, now found only in Ujung Kulon National Park. They have a greyish-brown skin that forms folds, giving them an almost armored appearance. Unlike their Sumatran cousins, Javan rhinos have only one horn, and this horn is typically only present in males. They are extremely shy creatures that prefer the dense vegetation of the rainforest to avoid detection. Conservation efforts are critical as their entire wild population is concentrated in a single location, making them vulnerable to disease and natural disasters.
facts: Unlike Sumatran rhinos, Javan rhinos have only one horn (in males).
They are extremely shy and elusive, making them difficult for researchers to track.
They primarily feed on shoots, twigs, and young leaves of forest plants.
population_estimate: ~76-87 individuals (new calf recorded April 2024 in Ujung Kulon)

name: Sumatran Orangutan
description: Sumatran orangutans are highly intelligent great apes known for their striking reddish-brown hair and long arms. They spend nearly all of their lives in the forest canopy, making them the largest arboreal mammals in the world. These primates are known for their complex tool use and problem-solving abilities in the wild. They exhibit strong maternal bonds, with offspring staying with their mothers for several years to learn survival skills. Their population is declining rapidly due to the conversion of rainforests into palm oil plantations.
facts: They have the longest birth interval of any land mammal, giving birth every 7-9 years.
They build a new nest to sleep in every single night high in the canopy.
Their diet consists mainly of fruit (about 60%), but they also eat bark and soil.
population_estimate: ~13,000 individuals (stable but threatened by habitat loss)

name: Komodo Dragon
description: The Komodo dragon is the largest extant lizard species on Earth, endemic to the islands of Komodo National Park. They are apex predators that use a combination of stealth, strength, and a potent venom to hunt their prey. Their saliva contains proteins that prevent blood clotting, causing their prey to go into shock. They are highly territorial and can be seen competing for mates and food in the grasslands and forests. Despite their fame, they are listed as endangered due to rising sea levels and habitat fragmentation.
facts: They possess a complex venom that prevents blood clotting and causes a drop in blood pressure.
Females are capable of parthenogenesis, meaning they can produce offspring without a male.
They can swallow prey like mid-sized piglets whole.
population_estimate: ~3,300 individuals (UGM 2024 survey - urgent conservation needed)

name: Anoa
description: The anoa is a small, forest-dwelling buffalo endemic to the island of Sulawesi, often referred to as the midget buffalo. They are adapted to the thick tropical forests where their smaller size allows them to navigate dense undergrowth. These animals are generally solitary and can become quite aggressive when they feel threatened or cornered. They play a key role in their ecosystem by browsing on various plants and helping in seed dispersal. They are currently threatened by hunting and the loss of their forest habitats.
facts: They are the smallest wild cattle species in the world.
They are very territorial and can be aggressive if threatened.
They prefer dense forests and are often found near water sources.
population_estimate: Fewer than 5,000 individuals (endangered due to hunting and habitat loss)

name: Babirusa
description: The babirusa is a unique species of pig found in Sulawesi, most famous for the extraordinary tusks of the males. These tusks grow upward, curving back toward the forehead and sometimes piercing the snout. They are not typical pigs and prefer to spend more time in the forest and mud wallows than in open plains. Their diet is more specialized than other pigs, consisting heavily of fruits, leaves, and fungi. They are rare and protected under Indonesian law to prevent their extinction.
facts: The upper tusks of males can actually curve back and pierce their own skull if not worn down.
They are excellent swimmers and often wallow in mud to stay cool.
Unlike most pigs, they have a very specialized diet of fruits and leaves.
population_estimate: ~10,000 individuals (threatened by habitat degradation)

name: Tarsier
description: Tarsiers are tiny, nocturnal primates with enormous eyes and long, slender fingers found in Sulawesi. Their eyes are so large that they cannot move them in their sockets, but they can rotate their heads 180 degrees. They are highly specialized insectivores that leap from branch to branch with incredible precision. These primates are very sensitive to stress and often cannot survive in captivity, making wild conservation essential. They are key indicators of a healthy forest ecosystem due to their strict dietary and habitat needs.
facts: Their eyes are larger than their brain, allowing them to see exceptionally well in the dark.
They are the only primates capable of rotating their heads 180 degrees in either direction.
They are purely carnivorous, eating mainly insects and small lizards.
population_estimate: Data limited/uncertain (cryptic species with difficult monitoring)

name: Maleo
description: The maleo is a unique megapode bird from Sulawesi that exhibits a fascinating nesting behavior. Instead of incubating eggs with their own body heat, they bury them in volcanic sand or geothermal soil. The natural heat of the earth hatches the eggs over several weeks without parental intervention. Once hatched, the chicks must dig themselves out and are capable of flying and foraging immediately. This reliance on specific geothermal sites makes them highly vulnerable to habitat destruction and egg poaching.
facts: The parents do not sit on the eggs; instead, they rely on geothermal heat from the earth.
Chicks are fully developed and can fly almost immediately after hatching.
They have a distinct black plumage and a bony casque on their head.
population_estimate: 8,000-14,000 adults (declining due to habitat loss)

name: Cendrawasih
description: The Cendrawasih, or Birds of Paradise, are renowned for the most spectacular plumage and courtship displays in the avian world. Found primarily in New Guinea and neighboring islands, the males develop elaborate feathers to attract females. These displays often involve complex dances and vocalizations performed in specific forest clearings. They are essential to the rainforest as they feed on fruits and insects, contributing to forest regeneration. Many species are now threatened by the illegal wildlife trade due to the demand for their beautiful feathers.
facts: They are found primarily in New Guinea and surrounding islands.
Male birds perform complex courtship dances to attract females.
Many species have evolved incredibly specialized feathers that look like wires, ribbons, or fans.
population_estimate: 41 species in Indonesia, 37 in Papua (stable population trend)

name: Rafflesia arnoldii
description: Rafflesia arnoldii is the world's largest individual flower and is famous for its parasitic nature. It has no stems, leaves, or true roots, living instead entirely inside the tissues of a host vine. The plant only becomes visible when it produces a massive, reddish-brown flower that can reach one meter in diameter. It is known as the corpse flower because it emits a strong odor of decaying flesh to attract carrion flies for pollination. Because it relies on a specific host and has a low pollination rate, it is extremely rare and endangered.
facts: It is known as the 'corpse flower' because it smells like rotting flesh to attract carrion flies.
The flower can grow up to 1 meter in diameter and weigh up to 11 kilograms.
It lives as a parasite inside the vines of the genus Tetrastigma.
population_estimate: Very rare - exact population not quantified (found in 5 Southeast Asian countries)

name: Titan Arum
description: The Titan Arum is one of the world's tallest and most unusual floral blooms, native to the rainforests of Sumatra. It produces a massive inflorescence that can tower over three meters high, making it a sight to behold. Like the Rafflesia, it produces a foul smell of rotting meat to attract beetles and flies for pollination. The blooming process is rare and unpredictable, often taking years between each flower cycle. Once it blooms, the flower only lasts for a short period before collapsing, making it a prized find for nature enthusiasts.
facts: It produces a massive inflorescence that can reach over 3 meters in height.
The bloom is very rare and only lasts for a short period (usually 24-48 hours).
It uses its foul odor to attract pollinators like beetles and flies.
population_estimate: Very rare in wild - exact population not quantified (cultivated in botanical gardens)

name: Timor Deer
description: The Timor deer is a medium-sized deer species found across the Lesser Sunda Islands, including Komodo National Park. They serve as one of the primary prey sources for the Komodo dragon, maintaining a delicate balance in the ecosystem. These deer are well-adapted to the dry savannahs and scrublands of the region. They are social animals that often move in small herds to avoid predators. Although more common than the rhinos, they are still protected to ensure the survival of the apex predators that depend on them.
facts: They are the main food source for adult Komodo dragons.
They are highly agile and can navigate the rugged terrain of the islands.
They are endemic to the Lesser Sunda Islands region.
population_estimate: Fewer than 3,500 individuals (endangered due to hunting)

name: Asian Water Buffalo
description: The Asian water buffalo in Komodo National Park is a sturdy herbivore that prefers wallowing in mud to regulate its body temperature. They are powerful animals that graze on the grasses of the savannah and the edges of the forests. In the park, they provide a significant biomass for the Komodo dragons to hunt, especially the calves. They are highly social and form strong bonds within their herds for protection. Protecting these buffalo is crucial for the overall health of the national park's food chain.
facts: They spend hours wallowing in mud to protect their skin from insects and sun.
They are essential prey for the larger Komodo dragons.
They are known for their large, curved horns used for defense.
population_estimate: Less than 4,000 individuals (wild population - critically endangered)

name: Blue Pit Viper
description: The Blue Pit Viper is a striking snake species found in the Lesser Sunda Islands, including the shores of Komodo and Rinca. They are characterized by their vivid blue or turquoise scales, which help them blend into the foliage. These snakes are ambush predators that wait patiently for small mammals or birds to pass by. They possess heat-sensing pits that allow them to detect warm-blooded prey even in total darkness. While beautiful, they are venomous and play a vital role in controlling the rodent population in the park.
facts: They have heat-sensing pits to locate prey in the dark.
Their bright blue color is a rare trait among pit vipers.
They are endemic to the Lesser Sunda Islands region.
population_estimate: Population data not specifically quantified

name: Orange-footed Scrubfowl
description: The Orange-footed scrubfowl is a ground-dwelling bird found in the forests and scrublands of Komodo National Park. They are famous for building massive mounds of decomposing organic matter to incubate their eggs. By utilizing the heat generated by the rotting vegetation, they can keep their eggs at a constant temperature. The parents spend a great deal of time maintaining the mound, adding and removing soil to regulate the heat. This unique nesting strategy allows them to thrive in diverse tropical environments.
facts: They build huge compost mounds for incubating their eggs.
They use their beaks to carefully regulate the mound's temperature.
They are predominantly ground-dwelling and avoid flying unless necessary.

name: Crab-eating Macaque
description: The crab-eating macaque is a highly adaptable primate found across the islands of Komodo National Park. As their name suggests, they have a diverse diet that includes crabs, fruits, insects, and occasionally small animals. They live in complex social hierarchies and are known for their intelligence and problem-solving skills. In the park, they often interact with other wildlife and are a common sight for visitors. While widespread, they are protected in the park to maintain the natural biodiversity of the islands.
facts: They are omnivores with a particular fondness for crustaceans.
They have a highly developed social structure with dominant alpha males.
They are one of the most adaptable primate species in Southeast Asia.
population_estimate: Data variable - market surveys show 10,000-20,000 taken annually (common but threatened)

name: Komodo Rat
description: The Komodo rat is a nocturnal rodent endemic specifically to the islands of Komodo National Park. They are most active during the night, foraging for seeds, fruits, and small invertebrates in the undergrowth. Because they are endemic to such a small area, they are extremely rare and special to spot in the wild. They play an important role as a food source for the park's birds of prey and smaller reptiles. Their survival is closely tied to the preservation of the park's native forest fragments.
facts: They are endemic solely to the Komodo National Park region.
They are nocturnal and avoid human contact.
They are considered a rare find for wildlife researchers.
population_estimate: Extremely rare - exact population not quantified

name: Green Turtle
description: The Green turtle is one of the most common sea turtles found in Indonesian waters, often nesting on remote beaches. They are primarily herbivores as adults, feeding on seagrass and algae, which gives their fat a greenish color. These turtles travel vast distances between their feeding grounds and their nesting beaches. They are critical for maintaining the health of seagrass beds, which serve as nurseries for many fish species. However, they face threats from plastic pollution and the illegal trade of their eggs.
facts: They are primarily herbivores, feeding on seagrass and algae.
They migrate thousands of miles across oceans to return to their birth beaches.
They are listed as endangered due to habitat loss and pollution.
population_estimate: ~15,000 clutches per year (conservation success in Indonesia)

name: Hawksbill Turtle
description: The Hawksbill turtle is easily identified by its sharp, beak-like mouth and the beautiful overlapping scales on its shell. They are primarily found in coral reefs, where they feed on sponges and other reef organisms. By eating sponges, they prevent them from overgrowing the corals, thus maintaining the health of the reef. They are critically endangered, largely due to the demand for 'tortoiseshell' used in jewelry and ornaments. Their conservation is vital for the survival of the coral reef ecosystems they inhabit.
facts: They have a narrow, pointed beak used to extract sponges from reef crevices.
Their shells are highly prized for ornamental carving.
They are essential for maintaining the biodiversity of coral reefs.
population_estimate: Critically endangered - genetic studies ongoing in Java Sea

name: Olive Ridley
description: The Olive Ridley turtle is a smaller sea turtle known for its olive-green, heart-shaped shell. They are famous for their mass nesting events called 'arribadas', where thousands of females nest on a single beach simultaneously. This strategy is believed to reduce the risk of predation for the hatchlings. They are found in warmer waters and are often seen following schools of fish and squid. Despite their large numbers, they are threatened by bycatch in commercial fishing nets.
facts: They engage in mass nesting events known as 'arribadas'.
They have a more rounded shell compared to other sea turtles.
They are highly migratory and travel across the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
population_estimate: Sporadic arribadas reported in Indonesia (nesting behavior varies)

name: Loggerhead Turtle
description: The Loggerhead turtle is named for its exceptionally large head and powerful jaws, which allow it to crush hard-shelled prey. They primarily feed on crabs, whelks, and other mollusks found on the ocean floor. These turtles have a long lifespan and migrate across entire ocean basins during their juvenile years. They typically nest on sandy beaches in warmer climates, including several locations in Indonesia. They are vulnerable to entanglement in fishing gear and the loss of nesting beaches to coastal development.
facts: They have the strongest jaws of all sea turtle species.
They exhibit long-distance migrations across multiple ocean basins.
They primarily feed on benthic invertebrates like crabs.
population_estimate: Limited nesting data available in Indonesia (rare visitor)

name: Leatherback Turtle
description: The Leatherback is the largest of all living turtles and is unique for having a leathery skin instead of a hard bony shell. This adaptation allows them to dive to extreme depths in the ocean, far deeper than any other turtle. They feed almost exclusively on jellyfish, acting as a natural regulator for jellyfish populations. They are found in the widest range of all sea turtles, from tropical to sub-polar waters. They are critically endangered due to pollution, especially the ingestion of plastic bags that look like jellyfish.
facts: They are the only sea turtle species without a hard shell.
They can dive to depths of over 1,000 meters.
They are the largest turtle species, reaching lengths of up to 2 meters.
population_estimate: 229 nests recorded in 2024 (Jamursba Medi/Warmon major sites - conservation success)

name: Flatback Turtle
description: The Flatback turtle is a species of sea turtle that is primarily found in the waters around Australia and the western coast of Indonesia. As their name suggests, they have a flatter carapace than other sea turtles, which may help them navigate shallow coastal waters. They are less migratory than other species, spending most of their lives in the continental shelf regions. They feed on soft corals, sea sponges, and various mollusks. Because they stay in a limited area, they are particularly sensitive to local pollution and coastal development.
facts: They have a flatter shell compared to other sea turtle species.
They are the least migratory of all the sea turtle species.
They primarily inhabit shallow coastal waters and continental shelves.
population_estimate: 20,000-21,000 nesting females globally, limited data in Indonesia
